utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness is sworn, can I mention one thing. It will take 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The revised witness lists we issued in the Status Conference yesterday were unsatisfactory in several ways, not least that some of the shading is so dense you can hardly read the document, and the third part of the document needs updating in several respects. We will try and reissue a more useful document tomorrow, and I would suggest deferring working on the present document until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Ms. Bibles. Examined by Ms. Bibles:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Hrustanovic Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Monday of this week, did you meet with a member of the Registry to certify two statements that you've made regarding the events in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those statements -- one of the statements is dated the 7th of October, 1994, the other dated the 12th of November, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If he could be shown those statements, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the documents that you certified with the registrar on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd move to admit the 92 bis packet into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P530.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Hrustanovic is a long-term resident of the town of Bijeljina. Prior to the takeover of Bijeljina, he worked as a financial director for a large company there. His evidence, which is being presented via 92 bis, covers several relevant areas of the indictment with respect to Bijeljina. With respect to the takeover of Bijeljina, he and other members of the community had heard that Arkan and his men were nearby at Popovi on the Drina River. On the night of the 31st of March, 1992, he woke to the sound of gunfire. The shooting that began that night went on off and on for the next three to four days. During that time period, the Muslim residents were confined to their homes. Through phone conversations with family and friends and the rest of the municipality, Mr. Hrustanovic learned that the war had begun. Through the media, he learned that over 40 people had been killed. During the days that the shooting was going on, an armed Serb wearing a uniform controlled his neighbourhood. This individual was Goran Jelisic. He directed the residents to stay in their homes. This is the same Goran Jelisic who was convicted in this Tribunal. After the takeover, there were still restrictions on the movements of the Muslim residents of the municipality. Uniformed Serbs patrolled the streets. They stopped non-Serbs and checked their papers. Mr. Hrustanovic saw that many shop windows of businesses belonging to Bosniaks had been smashed. He was also told by a Serb friend that he himself had been on an execution list but that his colleague had removed him from that list. Over a period of time, there were mass dismissals of non-Serbs, with their positions being replaced by Serbs. In the end in Bijeljina, only irreplaceable non-Serbs were kept in their positions and they were kept under close supervision. With respect to the destruction or desecration of non-Orthodox symbols, this witness describes in his statements that there were substantial destruction of non-Orthodox symbols. The mosques of the municipality were destroyed and the interior of a Catholic church was desecrated. With respect to forced labour, Mr. Hrustanovic was detained on the 10th of August, 1993. He was forced to work digging trenches and fortifications on the frontlines of the VRS. This was at the location and just after the VRS pushed the Bosnian army back from Brcko. The detainees were told to find shelter in the bombed-out houses in the area. They lived without roofs, sanitary facilities, or running water. The only food that they ate was the leftovers from the VRS soldiers. One of the Muslim men from Bijeljina, Suljo Osmanovic, was killed when a Bosnian shell hit the area in which they were digging trenches. This group of detainees was driven back to Bijeljina, taken to the MUP headquarters to be registered before they were released on the 4th of September, 1993. And finally, Mr. Hrustanovic was forced out of the municipality in 1994. This began when he was summoned to the offices of a Vojkan Djurkovic, who wore a JNA uniform and intimidated Mr. Hrustanovic. This intimidation culminated with the order that he would have to leave the municipality and he had to decide whether he was leaving via the Drina River or whether he was going to go to Tuzla. Mr. Hrustanovic made it clear that he did not intend to leave Bijeljina. Over the following days and time period, the witness was harassed and badly beaten by Djurkovic's men. On the 22nd of August, Mr. Hrustanovic and his family were detained and taken away with other Muslim residents in a cattle truck towards Tuzla. They were held overnight and subjected to humiliating searches. In the end, this group of Muslims was forced to walk through no man's land to Bosnian-held territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hrustanovic, in paragraph 6 of your statement, you say that life in Bijeljina started to change after the death of President Tito; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he died in 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there were social changes that took place but that this could be noticed only by those who were susceptible to these changes. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that same paragraph and in that same context, you go on to say that the Bosniaks were suppressed from social, political, and economic fields of work, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that many Bosniaks simply did not see what was going on, what was happening around them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that these changes were also reflected in the fact that workers' salaries were not being paid out, that strikes were being held and so on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the economic and social problems that arose here?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: There were other things there besides social and economic problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, was it only the Muslims that went on strike and that didn't receive their salaries on time, or did these social and economic crises reflect on all workers, regardless of their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: It depended on the structure, on the companies and the ethnic make-up of the workers in those companies. So it wasn't only that there were social and economic problems. The Bosnians were being suppressed. They were being pushed out of high-ranking positions, and Serbs brought in to replace them. And all this evolved through the organisation of the League of Communists. The Bosnians were found to be unsuitable. And this made it easier for them to be replaced from the posts they held and to be replaced by Serbs. So during that period of time, in a very rapid succession, the Bosniaks were being fired and the Serbs appointed to their posts. And the mayor -- the president of the municipality became a Serb, so was the president of the League of Communists; he was a Serb too. And the head of MUP was a Serb. The command of the garrison was also a Serb. The director of the Zitopromet company was also a Serb, so was the director of the medical centre. He was a Serb too, not to enumerate all the others. All I can say in summing up if you were to ask me who was in what -- which Bosniak remained in his place and post in what company, I would be hard pressed to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just asking you something with respect to what you say in paragraph 7 of your statement, that the changes were reflected in the fact that salaries weren't being paid out on time and that the workers organised strikes. So all I'm asking you now is: Was it only the Muslims that suffered these problems and went on strike and didn't receive their salaries on time, or did this social and economic crisis affect everyone?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: It was primarily the work organisations that went on strike which had a majority of employees being Bosniaks. There was the Zenit factory, the Uzice factory. As I say, it was mostly in those work organisations that this happened, because we were linked to the Belgrade economy. Zenit, for example, the Zenit company was linked 100 per cent to Belgrade. It exported footwear to the Soviet Union. Through another company, Centro Textile, we found it very difficult to be paid out the money we had earned. So that, too, was a sign that the Bosniaks -- or rather, firms employing Bosniaks, a majority Bosniak labour force, was not being paid for their exports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the economic crisis -- what you're saying is that the Muslims bore the brunt of the economic crisis and the Serbs didn't feel the crisis at all? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, with respect to the events in Bijeljina, we have had a number of witnesses. And as this comes under 92 bis, I'm not going to go through those events again. We have heard a great deal about the events themselves. So if we were to repeat all that, then I'd have no time left to deliberate his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm not going to dwell on those events with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we say that -- if you take this course with witnesses, as you do with this one, we will understand the position and indeed encourage any saving of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have been forced to save time, because for 92 bis I have been allotted one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hrustanovic, in paragraph 10, you go on to say that on the 31st of March, 1992 at about 2100 hours you heard some sort of shooting and that you rang up your daughter-in-law in Janja and she said that the war had started. And then you phoned up some other friends and nobody knew what was going on and they told you that some people had already been killed. Is that what you say in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, what did your daughter-in-law tell you? Did the war break out in Bijeljina or Janja? Where was the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: She said that the war had started in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is Janja from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 11 and 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing was happening in Janja?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that none of your friends knew what was actually going on. How come they knew that some people had been killed, then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I first phoned Janja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where nothing was happening.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing was happening in Janja, but the telephone lines were linked and you could hear -- they said you could hear the shooting. I didn't hear the shooting myself, because I was sleeping at that time, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you heard the shooting, in paragraph 10. Now you say that you didn't hear any shooting. Did you hear it or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it towards the end, when it was a general chaos and I jumped up to see what was going on. I phoned Janja and some other people from Bijeljina, and then I put all that together, all the tales that were recounted. But anyway, there was -- you could hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who were the people around Bijeljina killed on the night of the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't say which people, but they said that some people had been killed. It was only the next day that through the information media we learnt that one, two, three, four, five, six -- actually, over 40 people had been killed, and that's when there was an information blockade, as far as we were concerned, that was put in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "for us," "we," who do you mean; the inhabitants of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the inhabitants of Bijeljina, because that was the third, fourth, or fifth day when the Majevica repeater was turned the other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in total?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in Bijeljina. Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: The figure bandied about is approximately 600 inhabitants as having been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that was the figure being manipulated or bandied about.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the speculations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, who were the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I can enumerate some of them. But of course there were whole lists of people, whole families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who killed them and where?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: They were killed mostly by Arkan's men and people from Captain Dragan's guards, the Chetniks of Vojvoda, Mile Blagic. Actually, on the 31st of March, they entered Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That seems to be somewhat different from the testimony of other witnesses, but let's leave that aside for the moment. In paragraph 11, you say that you were very cautious on the phone, as you had heard that your phones were being tapped.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All the lines were intertwined and you didn't know who was talking to who, who was on line. So it was difficult to actually have the person answer your telephone call, the person you wanted to speak to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was a breakdown in the switchboard system, I assume. How else can you explain this? Why would anybody else listen in to your telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it had been organised earlier on, in advance. It was no breakdown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Hrustanovic, what were you then? Which office did you hold then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the board for economic and financial affairs at the Zenit industry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were one of the directors in Zenit?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you exported footwear?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I was the deputy director of Elektro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would be the reason why would somebody have your phone tapped? What would be these secrets that somebody would want to find out?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: All the lines were mixed up. And now, who was tapping who or not, that is something I don't know, but I assume that some people were tapped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You assume that some people were tapped and you include yourself among those persons; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that Serbs had your telephone tapped?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who created this commotion in Bijeljina were certainly listening in, and those were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please: How did they do this? Was it only Serbs who were then employed, say, in the police in Bijeljina, at the public security centre in Bijeljina or in the post office, for instance? Was it only Serbs who were employed there, or were there Serbs, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Both were employed. But when those who I mentioned entered town, they took over all functions. So they suppressed all the Bosniaks, all the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say that the Bosniak Muslims were all replaced ages ago, after Tito's death, 1980.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not what was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I asked you at the beginning. Things had changed and that Muslims had been suppressed and dismissed, replaced, the Secretary of the League of Communists was a Serb and so on and so forth. In these events, the League of Communists did not exist?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't listen to this properly. I'm just saying what --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I listened to what you were saying just now. I'm not talking about what I read.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I heard you, and I hope everybody else did too, that you explained that the Secretary of the Municipal Committee of the League of Communists was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And at the post office, of course, people went on working there, not only Serbs but Muslims too. But on that 31st of March, in those three, four, or five days, when everything that happened happened in Bijeljina, they took over all positions there. Also guards were set up. Arkan did this, Kapetan Dragan too. So there were no Muslims there. So they could have done whatever they wanted to with the telephone lines. They could have tapped anybody's conversations. They always had some locals who were there to help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had some different pieces of information here confirmed by other witnesses too. It wasn't Kapetan Dragan at all. It was a Serb guard led by Mauzer, otherwise a citizen of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Mauzer only joined them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You say that the shooting went on for the next three or four days and that through the media you were being informed that you should stay at home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And every street had a commissioner of its own, and among others, they cautioned us not to go out and to stay at home. Among others, there was Dragan Jelisic, who covered the area. We are neighbours, otherwise. He came to see a friend whose house was right by mine. I went out of the house and he said, "No, no, no, go back to the house," something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You say that through the media you found out that about 40 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which media reported about this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: It was only Bijeljina Television. I think that this went through TV Sarajevo, and then that was interrupted too. Subsequently, we heard who all the persons who went missing were. Entire families became extinct in this way. They were killed in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had the opportunity of seeing all of this here, and it is quite different from what other statements say, but I'm not going to dwell on that now. But tell me, in terms of what you claim in paragraph 14, you say that "Able-bodied Bosniaks in 1992 received call-up papers to report to the army of Republika Srpska." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: First, they reported for mobilisation, general mobilisation. When it was proclaimed, we Muslims thought that this did not pertain to us. However, over a short period of time, all Muslims were called up separately to Novo Selo for this mobilisation. I did not respond, but many did. And afterwards, those who did respond started getting call-up papers and they were sent to frontlines. We, who did not respond to mobilisation, were treated quite differently. We were sent on these work obligations, but I call them prison, slavery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this pertained to both Serbs and Muslims? Those who were in the army did not have work obligation and those -- those who were not in the army had work obligation and those who were in the army did not have it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No Serbs had work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How many Muslims were there in the army of Republika Srpska, Muslims from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were quite a few. And for the most part, they were sent to Pelagicevo and to Posavina. They did not send them to Majevica and Teocak because up there they had many friends and there were family ties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not go into where they were being sent. But these Muslims who were in the army of Republika Srpska, they were armed too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any of the officers who were Muslims and who commanded some unit of the army of Republika Srpska from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I know two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, who are they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Pasaga Halilovic and Jahic Mujica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pasaga Halilovic, was he a commander of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a brigade but it was a bigger formation, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other Muslims were on these units? Thousands, hundreds, how many?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I could not really answer that, but there were quite a few Muslims who went to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, this other man you mentioned, what was he?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: He also had some kind of rank. He did not have a formation, but he was engaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also a Muslim? Also in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also an officer?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand what you've been saying, you did not respond to the mobilisation call-up.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I was treated differently. That's why they took me to dig trenches, communication trenches, and everything that was involved in the fortification of lines, as it is called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Hrustanovic. Because you did not report for mobilisation, did somebody arrest you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: There was such a possibility, but I avoided such a thing because I did not have any papers on me which would enable me to walk about freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you went out for work obligation so everybody could see you and you could not really avoid anyone if somebody did want to see you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I find this question a bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you avoided being arrested and you went for work obligation together with others, so you were not hiding anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was at home. And I got call-up papers that on the 10th of August, 1993 I should report at the school yard of the Fadil Jahic Spanac School, which is vis-a-vis the SUP, the MUP, call it what you will, and then they picked us up, 47 of us, 17 from Bijeljina and 30 from Janja, and they drove us to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They drove you out there to work; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, actually, in paragraph 15 that on the fifth day, since that has started, together with your neighbour you walked out into the street for the first time in order to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was only on the fifth day that you came to learn about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: We heard some details only then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then some Serbs in uniform returned you to your home because it was not safe in the street.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We found out only later how dangerous it was for us to go out like that. We could have been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these Serbs who returned you to your homes, sent you back, they did that so that you could avoid being exposed to gunfire or something like.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a neighbour, Jelisic, nicknamed Adolf. He had a friend there and he's the one who actually sent us back. But there were others with him, so that is why I'm saying it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They sent you back. But they did not mistreat you in the process in any way or insult you in any way.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: They did not. We were just sent back, so that we would crawl back into hiding in our houses, and it was very dangerous to walk about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Hrustanovic. You're a Muslim who practically spent his entire career in managerial positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When things started in Bijeljina, you were a deputy general manager, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were a prominent and respected member of the community in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 22 of your statement, you say that one of the characteristics of the Serb campaign aimed at intimidating the non-Serb population was the mass dismissal of non-Serbs from work. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were some who were irreplaceable, but my turn came soon too. We were all pushed away. Zenit was a difficult company, difficult, really difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent your entire career in Bijeljina in positions of director.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I was director of several companies at different times. I was also director of a catering enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bijeljina. Also the medical centre in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can see, nobody ever dismissed you or replaced you or mistreated you in the streets of Bijeljina, even during the time of the conflict, although any Serb could have recognised you since you were such a prominent citizen; isn't that right? You were a well-known person in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: That was my very own merit, because I was on good terms with everyone. I didn't step on any toes. So I could not have experienced any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What you mentioned in passing a few minutes ago, that it was only the irreplaceable non-Serbs who stayed at work, who kept their jobs, does that mean that the Serbs in Bijeljina were selective in that sense? They distinguished between replaceable and non-replaceable Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to say something what I meant. For example, in Zenit, a technologist cannot be found. He's not there. Everybody who worked in technology -- I mean, it was hard to find people like that, and such people were kept until others were trained or until others were brought from elsewhere, and so on. That's what I meant. At a given point in time, they were irreplaceable. If there is no other electrician available, then they would leave that electrician. If there was no other technologist, they would leave that technologist. So it meant that it was something special that they could not find right then in terms of an adequate replacement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that there weren't electricians or technologists who were Serbs and that's why Muslims kept these jobs?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I just mentioned electricians by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Hrustanovic. It's a bit strange that that is the only reason why Muslims kept their jobs, and then on the other hand you talk about their large number in the army of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina and you also talk about officials and officers in the army of Republika Srpska who were Muslims. Were they also irreplaceable?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They simply agreed to be loyal to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This Pasaga Halilovic who you mentioned, was he director of a company in Bijeljina before that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the director of Duvan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he director now?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as he finished his job, they got rid of him the way they got rid of me, the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so he was expelled from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now he's in Gradacac, in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 10th of August, as it says here in your statement, you were detained and taken to Omerbegovaca, near Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were you arrested or was this labour that was organised? When you say "detained," that means taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it can be treated, but we were picked up, the 47 of us, and we were driven off in that direction. It's the same as if I had been taken prisoner. That's why I said that this was a prison sentence for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so it was as if you had been arrested, the fact that you were taken out for labour.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody mistreat you there, beat you, threaten you with firearms or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: We did have such unpleasant situations, yes. Some people were beaten up, badly beaten. Some people were almost beaten to death. The colour of their faces was like this, like this black thing you can see here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Didn't you say yourself that conflicts and the campaign against Muslims started even earlier on? You say even in 1991 this was in full swing. Isn't that what you said? This campaign against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: The campaign, yes, but there were no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. A campaign. And you were a respected Muslim in Bijeljina, a prominent Muslim. That's not in question.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how is this possible that it was only as late as August 1993 that the Serbs detained you or arrested your or something like that, if you say that the persecution of Muslims had been going on for several years before that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Other Serbs came in. All the domicile Serbs were repressed and suppressed and nobody could even notice them, the ones that lived there, but they -- the Krajisnik, men from Krajina, came from Ilidza and other places. And then you couldn't distinguish between them. Nobody knew who was who in Bijeljina any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that on that occasion the Serbs made you responsible for a small group of some ten people; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in Omerbegovaca, Brcko, they divided us up into groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were the head of one of these groups; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And that was the first time I saw who was with me in the group, because before that I was in a state of shock and didn't know who the other people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what shocked you so much?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was shocked to have been taken away and humiliated and taken off to dig trenches and dugouts and fortify the frontlines of the army of Republika Srpska. That's what shocked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the course of all this, did anybody abuse you, beat you, mistreat you in any way?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Not me personally, but other people from my group, yes, they did. They did mistreat some of the others, one or two people actually, and one of those was killed, Suljo Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say in paragraph 26 that while you were at those positions, that Suljo Omeragic was killed. I made a note of that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: His surname was Osmanovic, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: And that happened on the 20th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just clear that point up. He lost his life and was killed by a shell that was shot from Muslim positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nobody actually killed him there on the spot, the Serbs who were with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: But let me explain how this came about. There were shifts and people were rotated. One shift would take over every two days or three days. And usually when one shift replaced another, some of those young men there from the army of Republika Srpska, those youngsters, if I can put it that way, and the army of Republika Srpska had a lot of weapons. They would start shooting at the positions of the lilies or, rather, the fighters belonging to the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And just as the shooting stopped on the part of the army of Republika Srpska, a shell hit -- a shell was shot by the lilies, the Ljiljans, the Bosnian side. And then the shell hit a large tree trunk, and this man was digging communicating trenches and he was hit by a shrapnel here in his forehead, and by the time they got him to the sanitary corps, he was already dead. He was taken, actually, to Belgrade. That's what we were told, at least. And he died. It was only when we returned home that his sisters asked where Suljo was, where their brother Suljo was. And then it was through the Red Cross that we found that he had been buried in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he died as the result of his wounds en route to hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, he was actually -- received a fatal wound during the Muslim attack on Serb positions, one can say.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: They weren't attacks. They were just provocations. These were -- the others would keep shooting, and then they'd just return fire on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So he died by the fire that was opened by the Muslim side; is that it, then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, up at those positions, there were a lot of Serbs, weren't there? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: On the Serb side, yes, but on the other side over there ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of course not on the Muslim side. But there were a lot of Serbs there too. So the shell could not have selectively chosen to kill Suljo Omeragic. It was that it targeted Serb positions and it so happened that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed at Serb positions. I could have been killed too. And today, when I recollect those days and those events, I don't know how we stayed alive, the six of them in uniform and the four of us who were digging trenches. But he was the only one actually killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these six uniformed persons, they were also Muslims, were they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see, Serbs. So there were only four Muslims and the rest, the other six, were Serbs in that locality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Six of them were soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska and they were in uniform, and we were the workers, the labourers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this, please: You came back on the 4th of September, 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spent up at those positions some time, around 23 or 24 days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: 26 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, 26 days. You weren't arrested during all that time and you weren't detained and held in custody either, were you? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, except that one time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, the one you gave to the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Tuzla on the 7th of October, 1994, you say that your brother died on the 20th of May, 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that his wife, according to that statement of yours, set up with another -- with a Serb, Dragutin Mackovic, and she had a liaison with that particular person while your brother was still alive. Is that right? And then your daughter-in-law, towards the end of 1993, left for France, and you say that this man Mackovic stayed on living in their house.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was then that your problems started with that house, because he didn't want to leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't the reason. The reason was that I -- that he wanted me to sign over the house to him. Whereas, the house was my property, I owned it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's get this straight. You entered into the conflict not on any ethnic grounds and basis but in a personal conflict and difference of views between your sister-in-law's lover and yourself; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, houses were being seized and he thought he would seize my house too, because she left him a piece of paper, a certificate, telling him to ask me to sign over the house to her, to my sister-in-law. And later on he would -- she would sign it over to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Your sister-in-law left him a certificate asking that the house be signed over to him, and she lived in the house while she was your brother's wife.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Probably that was the price she was asked to pay for him to take her out of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't suppose you want to say that somebody wanted to stop your sister-in-law from travelling. Well, tens of thousands of people travelled and left. There were tens of thousands of Muslim refugees in Serbia from Bosnia, let alone how many in other countries. Nobody stopped them from leaving. So who could stop your sister-in-law from leaving Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, your information is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, anyway, but we're not challenging the fact that your conflict was one of a personal nature and not an ethnic one. It wasn't an ethnic conflict, it was a personal conflict between you and him.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could say that it was ethnically based too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't suppose your sister-in-law lived conjugally with this Mackovic on an ethnic basis.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they lived together out of love.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then. In paragraph 31 of your statement, you mention a certain man by the name of Vojkan Djurkovic, if I've noted this down correctly. And he was somebody you didn't know. He was unknown to you but began to play an important part in your life, as you yourself say.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 35 that you would see Djurkovic wearing a JNA officer's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that Djurkovic was in fact a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was an officer or not, but he wore an officer's uniform, at any rate, and it was the uniform worn by JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the time you're talking about and talking about this Djurkovic, was there any JNA unit in Bijeljina at all at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't have access to the garrison. It was called Fadil Jahic Spanac at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in paragraph 38, you say that the next time you went to see him, his paramilitaries were there.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that they recognised you because one of his policemen used to come to your house. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to summon me and to convey this summons for me to go to Vojkan's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it clear, then, that he wasn't a JNA officer of any kind but that in fact he led some sort of paramilitary unit or para-police unit or member of the VRS or police or what? Tell me what he was in actual fact. What was he?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: He was at the head and led that commission, the commission that was called the Commission for Exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: But he wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. But everybody wore a uniform. But he's from Bijeljina otherwise; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: He was from a village, Latoma [phoen] is the name of the village. It's nearby, quite near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But we can say that he was from Bijeljina municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not from the town itself but from a nearby village; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that Djurkovic exerted pressure upon you to leave Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: This man Djurkovic and that other one that I mentioned a moment ago, Mackovic, with whom you had that disagreement, the two of them were friends; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were, were they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to go back to Mackovic for a moment he didn't ask you to give him something. It was your sister-in-law who left him a chit authorising him to have the house signed over to her, the one that belonged to your brother.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But then she would have signed it over to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what would have been, we can't really know, but she left this piece of paper and -- instructing you to sign over the house to her. So is this an inter-ethnic conflict or was it a conflict within a personal relationship?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything was on a national ethnic basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, everything on an ethnic basis. All right. Now, several days later, you and your family in the presence of this man Djurkovic were sent by truck to territory under the control of the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, according to what you say in your statement given to the security centre in Tuzla, a Serb by the name of Vujadin informed you of all this. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me to beware of Dragutin, to be wary of Dragutin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which Dragutin, Mackovic or Djurkovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Mackovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was the person who was living with your sister-in-law but they weren't married.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me to be wary because he went around saying to Vujadin that he would send me off to do forced labour, work duty, and that he'd find somebody there to shoot me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, according to your statement, that was all in May 1994. That's when all that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Did you report him to the local police station, then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, you were confident that the police would protect you. Was it -- were the policemen Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I made a cardinal mistake there, for reporting this, because they were all the same people. They were prosecutor and judge in one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that some unknown person stormed your house, beat you up, and forced you to leave your home.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And all this was done continuously. It was a series of events forcing me to leave Bijeljina, because I had previously told Vojkan that I wouldn't leave Bijeljina dead or alive, that I had no intention of moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But is it true that you reported the event to the security centre in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was the Serbs who manned that security centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that the policeman performed his duty professionally, he compiled a report in the proper manner, that he was very proper in his conduct? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell him that Vojkan Djurkovic had been forcing you to leave your house, or did you just give a description of the men that on the 30th of May forced you to -- mistreated you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I just mentioned the man that was nicknamed Rosavi with a bad complexion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you described the people that mistreated you. You didn't say that it was Djurkovic in actual fact who was forcing you to leave Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: But all this took place through Djurkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But you didn't report that to the policemen in Bijeljina. You just described the people who mistreated you when they stormed your house.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was making this statement in the police station not in just one or two sentences. I made a complete statement narrating what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On the 22nd of August, 1994, Djurkovic expelled you and your family to territory that was under Muslim control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd, he rounded us up and it was only on the 24th that I crossed over into territory under the control of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was with him? Tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: With Vojkan, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a policeman with white belts, bandoliers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean a traffic policeman, actually, wearing these white belts? Because that's what the traffic police wore, is that right, these white belts?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not well versed in matters of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that another 161 persons together with you left Bijeljina on that occasion. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: 35 of us were rounded up on the 22nd, and we were taken to the Fazanerija in Suho Polje. And the next day these other 161 persons turned up. They were brought in in two busloads, and it was only at 1600 hours, after having been examined and checked, were we sent in two trucks via Priboj to Lopare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. From what you're saying now - and you're mentioning -- you've mentioned these 161 persons who left with you - it would appear that they left Bijeljina of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody left Bijeljina of their own free will, in actual fact, but they had to pay a very high price to Vojkan Djurkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean they bribed Djurkovic to allow them to leave Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to avoid being beaten, like I was. So they would have to pay Djurkovic some money, as much as each of them could, and then they were allowed to take something with them, some belongings with them in a bag; whereas I myself had to leave with a plastic bag, that was all, and all I could get into that plastic bag was a change of clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means they didn't let you take your things with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No. None of us who had been rounded up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, on the basis of what you've been saying now, nobody expelled you. On the contrary, you say that they had to give bribes in order to be able to leave. Now, let's clarify this, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say "bribe."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that they gave money allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: They were bargaining with Vojkan, depending on who should give how much money and then be transferred across the lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In view of what you explained just now, Djurkovic, Mackovic, your relations with Mackovic, doesn't it seem to you, Mr. Hrustanovic, that the reason for your departure was of a completely different nature? It wasn't expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what nature?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Personal conflict.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one you had with this Mackovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No personal conflict, no way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If it's not, that's what you're saying. Of course, I'm not going to squabble with you over that. And tell me, this Djurkovic you mention, who was allegedly the organiser of these expulsions, did he belong to a political organisation in the area of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he belonged to the Serb Unity, something like that. That was the name of the party more or less, Arkan's party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, he was not a member of the army of Republika Srpska or of the police, nothing. He was a self-styled mediator there. There was a Commission for Exchanges that was led by a completely different person officially.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: He was this official person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But there is information to that effect. But since he was not a member of any army or police, does the same go for Mackovic? Was Mackovic a member of any army or police?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: It says in my statement that Mackovic was not a member of any formation but he was in the executive committee of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem to you, Mr. Hrustanovic, that you are actually the victim of a criminal group, a group of criminals, not a campaign orchestrated by Serbs against you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not the only victim. 30.000 inhabitants, that was the population of Bijeljina. And everybody was expelled. Only 5 per cent of the Muslims were kept. So we were all victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not testifying about that, how many Muslims remained. You do know that a great many Muslims nowadays live and work in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I know how they live in Bijeljina, these 5 per cent who stayed behind, this 800 to 2.000 persons. They cannot even be seen. They do not live in their own houses. They lived in auxiliary buildings, in sheds, garages, basements, cellars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not yet. I didn't manage to get my property back. I live in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you in Bijeljina recently? Have you been there recently?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was an assemblyman there in the first Assembly after Dayton, 1997-1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were an assemblyman. How many more Muslim assemblymen were there in Bijeljina who were elected there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: There were 12 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of a total of how many assemblymen in the municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Sixty; 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: There should have been many more of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then and from then on, did you think that there was no discrimination against the Muslims by the Serbs in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: We were just there as ikebana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you did not carry out your duties?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, we were just ikebana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody exert any pressure against you, while you were an assemblyman? Did somebody exert any pressure against you as a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody exerted any pressure, but quite simply nothing we proposed was taken into account. And what we asked for, and what we had the right to ask for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But when the war was over and when you were in Bijeljina again and you were even a member of the Assembly, did you raise the issue of Mackovic's and Djurkovic's responsibility, if you thought that what was done to you was done in an illegal way by violating your rights or something like that? Did you bring any charges against them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have anyone to complain to. But once conditions are created for me to take action, I shall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. Are you finished? Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will really try to finish within a few minutes' time. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to ask Mr. Hrustanovic: You gave two statements. This first statement you gave as far back as 1994. In paragraph 3, it reflects what you said, and in this third paragraph it says, "My problems in Bijeljina started only after the death of my brother." This statement, therefore, shows that you personally did not have any problems until May 1993, the 20th of May, 1993. That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any problems. I had a very correct relationship with my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then today, in response to somebody's question - I don't know whose exactly - you said approximately that many people from Ilidza and Krajina came and that they took over a great many things in town.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges where they came from and how many of them were there? Because they had left their homes somewhere else. Do you know that or do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the number. I know that people from elsewhere took all key positions in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know where they came from? So from Krajina and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: Usually people said that they were from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more thing: In the summary here, when you spoke to the Prosecutors, you said that there were 40 victims during that gunfire in Bijeljina, and that's what you said in the statement that you gave to the investigators. I am sorry if I made a mistake here, but I think that you said today that in Bijeljina, in the month of March, 600 people were killed? Did I hear this well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll explain. The media reported that figure, 40. And we were under an information blockade, and only later, when we were able to move about, when we could hear what was going on in the area, the speculation is that 600 Bosniaks were killed in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month of March that year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HRUSTANOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of March that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hrustanovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now, until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of September, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
